title: How to calculate "inherit velocity" with simulation nodes particles
body_html:
I want to calculate the velocity of each point on an object's surface in world coordinates and store that in a named attribute so that particles emitted from this surface can inherit the velocity of the surface. This surface velocity needs to be based on world space - ie include the whole object's translational velocity and rotations that contribute to the velocity. I want to use simulation nodes rather than Blender's built in particles as there are other effects I need to add in on top of this.

Current File:
answer_html:
(Using Blender 3.6.8)

Approach

The velocity in the world coordinates of the emitting object is computed and stored as an attribute by a GeometryNodes modifier attached to this object. The achieved field is processed by an other object, using an other GeometryNodes modifier.

This figure illustrates the "Object to track" motion while it is translating along the Y axis and rotating around the Z axis, starting from the world origin. Elongated cones are visualizing the instantaneous velocity vector in world coordinates of each corner of the cube. Tetrahedra are visualizing the successive position of the initial top right corner sampled every 5 frames. The velocity vector must be tangent to such a trajectory, and its magnitude must be proportional to the distance between two adjacent tetrahedra.

GeometryNodes modifiers

Emitter:

The above GN graph, attached to the emitting object, is only storing named attributes. The velocity is computed as the difference between positions at two successive frames using a Simulation Zone.
1. The previous frame position is stored in Point domain as an attribute named "old". It is initialized with the Position at frame 1, upstream of the Simulation Zone.
2. Accordingly, the named attribute "velocity" is initialized null.
3. The instantaneous Location and Rotation of the emitting object are recovered in the world coordinates, using an Object Info node connected to a Self Object node. To do so, the Transform Space is set to Original.
4. The emitting object, whose geometry is invariant in its own GeometryNodes modifier, is rotated then translated using a Transform Geometry node.
5. This transformed geometry is not connected to the Group Output node. It is instead used to transfer, to the simulation zone, the instantaneous Position of the emitting object vertices, using a Sample Index node.
6. To these current positions are subtracted the "old" ones to compute the "velocity".
7. Eventually, current positions are stored as "old" for the next frame.

Observer:

The above GN graph is attached to a fixed object acting as an observer, taking advantage of the vertices position and of the "velocity" field of the emitting object.
About the position: (part in green)
1. A tetrahedron (i.e. a Cone with 3 vertices) is dynamically added to the output geometry using a Simulation Zone made of a single Join Geometry node.
2. Sampling is controlled with a Switch node. A new tetrahedron is added every 5 frames, identified with a Modulo math node, starting at frame 1.
3. The tetrahedron position is set using an Instance on Points node.
4. This position is copied from the emitting object vertex of Index 0. This single point is chosen through the Selection socket connected to an Equal compare node.
5. The Geometry of the emitting object (and so the current position of its vertices) is recovered through an Object Info node. The Transform Space is set to Relative "to maintain the relative position between the two objects in the scene". Because the observer is fixed while the emitting object is moving, the current position of the seeding point is changing in time.
About the velocity: (part in blue)
6. An elongated cone is positioned, downstream of the Simulation Zone, at each vertex of the emitting object using as previously an Instance on Points node connected to an Object Info node set in Relative Transform Space.
7. Using an Align Euler to Vector node, the Z axis of instanced cones is aligned to the "velocity" vector recovered from the point they are attached to, through a Named Attribute node.
8. The same attribute is used to scale instanced cones Z axis, to make these length proportional to the "velocity" magnitude (NB: The factor 30 to scale the length was adjusted to fit the demonstration case ; it has no meaning).
9. Because the observer is fixed in the scene, this illustrates that the "velocity" field stored as attribute in the emitting object is indeed in the world coordinates, and not in the object coordinates. The resulting animation is insensitive to the position and the rotation of the observer.

Resources

Benchmark

Lutzi proposal is based on vector algebra instead of a Transform Geometry node to apply rotation and translation. The following GeometryNodes graph is timing both approaches when the objective is to store a position field as an attribute. It is attached to a point cloud with 100.000 elements.

Vector algebra:

1. The rotation is computed with a Vector Rotate node.
2. The translation is computed with an Add vector math node, providing the sought field.

Geometry transformation:

1. The rotation, then the translation, are computed by a single Transform Geometry node.
2. The sought field is recovered through a Sample Index node set in Point domain and connected to a Position node.

Conclusion:
Repeated runs show that the "Geometry transformation" approach is 1.5 to 2.0 times faster than the "Vector algebra" one. One explanation is that for a uniform transformation (i.e. with the same parameters for all vertices), the Transform Geometry node is optimized, counterbalancing the extra Sample Index node cost. But it can not apply a "per vertex" specific transformation as its Translation, Rotation and Scale sockets are not fields.

title: Geometry Nodes - Weight Paint is not affecting "Set Position" smooth
body_html:
I am trying to make a procedural terrain with GeoNodes. My weight paint is not affecting the Set Positions Node in the way, that it takes any weights into account for the translation/sculpting. It is only taking the group as a whole for that gruff and bold effect. And despite the facts the different weight-zones are perfectly working for example with the density of distributed points or the scale of instances.

I also tried to pipe the attribute into the Z value of the Offset. But it resulted in the same issue. I am working with Blender 3.2.

Am I missing something?
answer_html:
The data type of the selection socket is boolean, so it's values will be either 0 or 1 (false or true). Float values are internally converted to boolean using the condition $X \gt 0$.

If what you want is to control what percentage of the translation will be applied, you will need to multiply the translation by the weight:

the color of a socket shows what data type it works with, if you can't see the difference (or it's really hard to see) between a float socket and a boolean socket (and maybe string sockets), you may have some colorblindness similar to mine.

The Blender documentation says that float sockets are gray, while booleans are pink:

Float (gray):

Indicates numeric value’s information. It can either be a single numerical value or a so-called “value map”. (You can think of a value map as a gray-scale map where the different amount of bright/dark reflects the value for each point.) If a single value is used as an input for a “value map” socket, all points of the map are set to this same value. Common use: Alpha maps and value options for a node.

Boolean (pink):

Used to pass a true or false value.

title: Take position values geometry nodes and apply them on an object outside of geometry nodes
body_html:
I am trying to figure out how to take values that I have exposed in the group output in geometry nodes/stored as named attributes and take these values and use them elsewhere in a different object as it's transform.

Here I have the values that are in the geometry nodes spreadsheet, so I know that they are being written, though I am having difficulty taking these out of geometry nodes and on direct XYZ transformations on a different object. The goal is to have a camera follow the center of the bounding box of the geometry nodes, and my workaround was to have an object get moved to the center of said bounding box with these values.

In the modifier information I can also see that the named attributes are also being exposed, though I am unsure where to go form here.
answer_html:
(Using Blender 4.2.1)

This proposal is an adaptation of the post Passing GeoNodes attribute to Shader frame offset.

Approach

The overall objective is to track with a camera the center of the bounding box of an object. One approach is to add a third object (named "Coder" thereafter) between the object to track and the tracking camera. Its purpose is to make the communication between both

  • by computing the bounding box center (receive)
  • by providing this position to the camera (send)

Coder setup

1. In Object Mode, add an object made of one vertex using the menu entry Add>Mesh>Single Vert>Add Single Vert. Its position is irrelevant.
2. Add a GeometryNodes modifier to this object, with the above graph.
3. The object to track (named "Suzanne" here) is provided through the GN modifier input parameters.
4. Its bounding box center coordinates are computed from its geometry recovered through an Object Info node whose Transform Space is set to Relative.
5. The single point of the "Coder" is moved with a Set Position node to the location computed at step 4 (see the light orange dot in the 3D Viewport). It is to notice that only the position of the vertex is updated. The object's origin remains at its creation location defined at step 1. To use this vertex as a moving point in the definition of a constraint, the documentation explains that "(...) the constraint will target the median point of this vertex group instead of the object’s origin".
6. Consequently in Edit Mode, in the Object Data Properties panel, add a Vertex Group (named "Coder") and Assign to this group the single vertex after selecting it. With only one point, the group median point is this point.

Camera setup


(In this figure, the "Coder" is displayed as a black dot at the center of the camera view)
7. Add a Damped Track constraint to the camera. Set the Target to the "Coder" object created at step 1, then the Vertex Group to the "Coder" group created at step 6.
8. Adjust the Track Axis.

Resources

As you can see below, the geometry being plugged in below clearly shows a branch with the leaves attached to it:

but when I attempt to instance that onto the main trunk curve, the leaves disappear:

file: (version 4.3)
answer_html:
The real reason you can't see the leaves is not because you did something wrong in your setup or the leaves are in the wrong position. All your geometry is still "there", with all the leaves placed correctly, you just can't see them. And the real reason for this is that you have a big "instance tree" in which you have multiple nested instances:

There is a limit on the number of nested instances, after which blender will simply delete (or hide) all child instances. This is written in the official documentation: I'm not sure why you actually went over 8 levels, since it looks like you have less levels. It might be because I just don't understand what they actually mean by "level", it seems like the fact that each instance has both nested instances and mesh data increases the nesting level, so if you use a Geometry to Instance node on all your mesh data before applying it to the Join Geometry node it will fix the issue.

Another solution (which they actually suggest) is to use the Realize Instances node to reduce the nesting.

But again, if you use a Geometry to Instance node after each Curve to Mesh node (in your case), you'll fix the problem and effectively only have about 5-6 levels. That's the amount I'd actually expect you to have without all that manipulations, but again, for some reason, that's not the case.

title: How to cache Simulation Zone in Scene Strip for correct VSE rendering?
body_html:
I'm currently using this node setup to count numbers, which utilizes the Simulation Zone node. This scene (Counter Scene) is added to the VSE via a Scene Strip inside the Edit Scene. I noticed that the violet bar at the bottom of the Counter Scene dopesheet needs to be solid violet, as shown in the green circle, rather than the diagonally striped violet shown in the red circle, for the counting numbers to render correctly.

Currently, the only workaround I’ve found to get the solid violet bar is to go to the Counter Scene, position the timeline at frame 0, then press and hold the right arrow key until the entire animation strip completes — which can take some time. After that, the bar appears solid violet and now it also displays the animation correctly in the Edit Scene.

Is it possible to "cache" this instantly, or is this workaround the only option? I had assumed that rendering the VSE timeline with its Scene Strips included would render everything correctly. Since rendering starts from frame 0, I expected the Simulation Zone to evaluate each frame properly as it renders, with each subsequent frame being updated accordingly. However, it appears that the render does not work correctly if the violet bar in the Counter Scene is not solid.
answer_html: The diagonally striped violet bar indicates that the Simulation Zone has not been cached yet, which is why the Scene Strip does not render correctly in the VSE unless you manually scrub the timeline from frame 0. Scene Strips do not automatically evaluate Simulation Zones frame by frame during rendering unless a cache already exists, so rendering the VSE alone is not sufficient. The correct solution is to bake the simulation. This can be done either by adding a Bake node after the Simulation Zone, which caches the simulation results and makes them immediately available for VSE rendering, or by using the Bake button directly on the Simulation Zone node itself in the Geometry Nodes sidebar, accessible with the N key when the Simulation Zone node is selected. As Lutzi notes, you will need to re-bake whenever anything upstream of the Simulation Zone changes, and it is generally best practice to place the Bake node as far upstream as possible so that only the necessary parts are baked. Alternatively, as Gordon Brinkmann points out, baking directly from the Simulation Zone node allows you to cache only that specific zone while keeping the rest of the node tree dynamic.

title: Maze Generation with Geometry Nodes and Simulation Nodes - Attribute Updating Issue
body_html:
I'm currently working on a maze generator project using Geometry Nodes and Simulation Nodes, inspired by Daniel Shiffman's tutorial and the corresponding code. I've made good progress so far but have encountered a challenge when trying to update attributes based on a condition, similar to the removeWalls function in the sketch.js example.

Here's the specific problem I'm facing:

I have a grid of cells, and for each cell, I've initialized four boolean attributes: topWall, rightWall,bottomWall, and leftWall. These attributes represent whether walls exist in each direction and are initially set to True for all cells.

I've also stored the coordinates of neighboring cells in attributes for each cell. This allows me to look up the attributes of neighboring cells easily.

Now, my goal is to determine which cell is the current active cell and which one is the next cell. Based on this determination, I need to remove the walls between these cells.

I've successfully removed walls from visited cells gradually over time as the simulation runs. However, the challenge arises when I need to remove walls only between the active/current cell and the next cell. I can't update by directly plugging the condition into the value socket of my boolean attributes every frame because the condition for wall removal may or may not be met, causing the attribute values to fluctuate.

My idea to address this issue is to only store the updated attribute when the condition for wall removal is met. If the condition isn't met, I want to retain the attribute values from the previous simulation cycle. The problem is that the Switch node doesn't accept fields as input.

I have to do this for all neighbor pairs of course:

I believe the solution to this problem might be relatively straightforward, but somehow I cannot wrap my head around it. Also, I am not sure how ell this question is suited for this forum. Any guidance or suggestions on how to manage attribute updates based on conditions in Geometry Nodes would be greatly appreciated.

Here is the blend file
answer_html:
If you use the structure of the mesh to store the variables, while keeping the current index separate from the mesh data, things become simpler $\tiny\text{I think...}$.

We start with some mesh, like a grid, in which each face will be a cell, and edges will be walls.

First we choose a random face to start and mark it as visited:

Mark all edges initially as walls:

A good thing to have is precomputed neighboring faces indices so there's easy access to to them. For a face, we can store each neighbor's index on each corner of the face, since the number of corners and neighboring faces is the same (ignoring borders).

To store the indices of neighbors we need first to get those values. With the Edges of Corner node we can get the next edge index (next is the edge after the corner in face winding order), then we use the Corners of Edge to get the corner of the neighboring face (if the first corner is the current corner, switch to the next corner), from that we just use the Face of Corner node to get the index of the neighboring face.

Visualisation:

On node tree:

Store also the index of the edge between the face and it's neighbor:

Now we start the Simulation Zone:

Its inputs are:

  • Unvisited faces (Integer) : Number of faces not visited, starts as the number of faces - $1$ (for the one that was chosen for starting).
  • Geometry (Geometry) : The mesh being operated.
  • Stack (Geometry) : Store previously visited indices as points with ID set to the index. Starts empty.
  • Current (Integer) : Index of the current cell, the one chosen randomly at the start.

First in the simulation we only want it to run if there are still unvisited cells, so check if the number of unvisited faces is $0$ to skip the simulation:

To get the non visited neighbors of the current face, get only its face corners and, sampling from the mesh the 'visited' attribute, delete the ones that point to visited faces:

Now we need two branches of nodes, one for when there's unvisited neighbors, and other for when there isn't.

For when there is, get the stored neighbor index of a randomly selected unvisited neighbor and mark it as visited, this will be the new current. From the same, get the stored edge index for the edge between and unmark it from being a wall. Also, store the old current on the stack as the ID of a new point:

For when there is no unvisited neighbors, remove the most recent from the stack and get its face index stored in the ID, that is the new current. The mesh remains unchanged:

Finally we switch between the values of when there's unvisited neighbors and when there isn't by checking the amount of unvisited neighbors, we also decrease the amount of total unvisited faces only if there were unvisited neighbors:

After that you can use the attributes to select which edges or faces will get instances, material or whatever you want.

Full node tree:

Edge cases: The reason there's no need to check for border edges is that the neighbor storing method stores the index of the actual face when there's no neighbor for a corner, but in the simulation when getting the unvisited neighbors it is discarded since the current is already selected.

$\small\text{Blender 4.0}$

This method works on any mesh that has a single mesh island where all edges have one or two faces.

title: Why does each point have the same life time?
body_html: Why does each point have the same life time? I would expect like, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 etc. (one new point each frame, and life time increments by one...)
answer_html:
Take a close look at the sockets of Life Time. It's always a green diamond with a dot in the middle. From the docs:

Diamond with Dot: The socket can be a field, but it is currently a single value. This is helpful because it allows tracking where single values are calculated, instead of a field with many different results.

This means that you assign the same life time value to every new point you join to the simulation. You need to make that property a field. From your description i assume you want to increment Life Time of every existing point by $1$ per frame and let every new point start with Life Time = 0. Try this setup:

As you can see, the simulation is at frame 21 and the first point (index 0) has a Life Time value of $21$. Also observe that the sockets of Life Time have changed to a filled diamond, indicating a real field.

(Side note: i am not sure why you plugged the point Geometry output node into the simulation Geometry input node. Makes not much of a difference except for a duplicated first point if i am not mistaken.)

title: Hit fx with geometry nodes
body_html:
I am following a video about a hit effect with Geometry Nodes.

The hit effect shown in the video is created by a bunch of transparent planes and some particles. The one-minute video is not a tutorial, but rather a process documentation with a few keywords. The first part shows the creation of the image textures with Material Maker, then the creation of the explosion in Blender with Geometry Nodes, and finally the addition of the animated particles.

Although, I basically got stuck pretty early because of my lack of knowledge in Geometry Nodes and I'd appreciate if someone could tell me which nodes to use and why. This is what I got so far:

Geometry Nodes:

Material Shader:
answer_html:
There was a similar question about this video but it was closed or deleted because it was too broad. Let's focus on the middle part here:

The Creation of The Explosion With a Bunch of Planes

This effect can be created with a few Geometry Nodes and a material. In my humble opinion, it would be easier to use one or more planes for the instances. This has the advantage that you already have a UV map and can easily set the origin and the material and saves you a few nodes. It would also be easier to use an individual image texture for each "explosion variant" instead of four variants on one image. This would save you the UV vector math calculations. But well, let's stick to the video.

1. The Creation The Plane Instances

You have already done this with a Grid node. Here, it's important that you need to set the origin to the bottom center of the plane so the images are aligned properly. Use the Set Position node with offset y: 0.5 m the get the origin right.

As you have already done and as described in the documentation, you also need a Set Material node to assign the material and a Store Named Attribute node to save the generated UV map in an attribute. It's uvs in the example.

Finally, create the instances on a point cloud with a Points node and an Instance on Points node. The first node creates several points, all at the same position and the other node places the planes on the points. The origin determines the position during creation, which means that all planes are stacked in the same place.

Last but not least, add a Random Value node and connect it with the Rotation input of the Instance on Points node. Set the Min and Max to -pi and pi (Blender will replace it by 3.142). Now the planes are rotated by min -180° and max 180° in all directions.

2. The Animation of The Explosion

This is just done by increasing the Scale value of the Instance on Points input from 0 to ... however large you want it to be. I've done it with a driver. It's created automatically when you enter a value that starts with a #. Then the input box turns purple. Try #min((frame/25)**2.5, 20). It scales the planes exponentially from a very low scale to a maximum of 20. There is another driver in the material shader to control the transparency.

3. The Material Shader

Here you need assign each instance plane a random image texture. In the video an image as four variants on it, so it requires some math to shift the UVs and do the random pick.

Fading out is done by increasing the transparency in the material shader using a driver (expression is simply #frame) and two Map Range node plus a Float Curve to let it glow for a long time and then let it go out quickly.

If you want to try at home, here's the used image texture. It's a white image on transparent/white background = nothing to see.

title: Why do evaluations on different domains produce such different results?
body_html:
Face corner has always been a concept that confuses me. Every time I use it, I am confused by its illogical results.

How can I understand the difference between them? When I input index, the results are inconsistent with those from the face of corner.
answer_html:
If you have a triangulated square and want to color it in such a way:

Imgur mirror* Imgur mirror

In game engines you will do it by having separate triangles, that is by using 6 vertices, not 4. In Blender you would do it by splitting the diagonal edge. Now you can save the red color to the vertices of the long edge belonging to the top triangle, and cyan color to the verts of the long edge belonging to the bottom triangle.

However Blender makes such tasks easier in various ways. In this case, you can use a face corner domain, and since each face has its own face corners, not shared with other faces, the diagonal edge of the square, while (like any single edge) uses only 2 vertices, it has (assuming it's connected to only 2 faces, as in usual manifold geometry) 4 face corners, a pair on each side. So on one side you store cyan color, on the other side red color, the effect is accomplished.

It's not the case just with color, I think most commonly you will see this in case of UV Map seams, though in game engines the vertices are also duplicated for e.g. material boundaries.

Now in your specific case, You're using a "Set Position" node. That node sets position of cloud points/instances/vertices (emphasis as that's what you have in this case). Then you tell Geometry Nodes to evaluate on face corner domain instead, but since there isn't a 1:1 vertex:corner relation (a vertex can have multiple face corners associated with it - as many, as the number of faces using this vertex), you need to either replace the "Evaluate on Domain" node with "Evaluate at Index" to specify which corner you mean, or deal with the consequences of an interpolation.

An interpolation is an average of all elements of left (connected from the left) domain associated with the element of the right domain (the currently evaluated element), except for boolean type, as is the case here. A boolean interpolation rules are described here:

Blender Documentation: Attributes: Attribute Domains: Boolean Domain Interpolation

If you're confused with e.g. "currently evaluated element", this series of posts of mine may help you:

  • Combine two position nodes (uses Transfer Attribute, non-existent in B3.4+, but the logic of evaluation is still the same)
  • Raycast + Align Euler to Vector. Wrong Hit Normals
  • What Does Capture Attribute Add to Geometry
  • Understanding how "vertex of corner" works in geometry node
  • Passing Data Into Simulation Zone

* - SE image hosting has problems

title: Copy attribute frome edge to face
body_html: I have a question that is probably very basic for most of you, but that I'm stuck on. I have a starting mesh that contains a edge marked by an attribute (in this case “test”). After extruding the edge of the mesh, I'd like to “transfer” the attribute of the marked edge to its extruded face
answer_html:
(Using Blender 3.6.8)

The attribute is already "transferred" to the extruded face:

1. The Store Named Attribute node is tagging True a single edge chosen through its Selection socket.
2. The Extrude Mesh node set in Edges mode is preserving the attribute value when it is copying edges before translating these.
3. The attribute value for connecting edges (those "vertical" in the demonstration case) is copied from the original vertex they are extruded from. Because of special interpolation rules for boolean, such a vertex is True if any of its connected edges is True.
4. So, all 4 edges of the face of interest are tagged True. Consequently, because of the same rules, the face is tagged True.
NB: Beware that if Float instead of Boolean type is used, with 0 instead of False and 1 instead of True, the "vertical" edges value is $0.5=\frac{1}{2}(0+1)$ and the face of interest value is $0.75=\frac{1}{4}(1+1+0.5+0.5)$, not $1$.

title: An object that stretches between two other objects?
body_html:
I'm modeling furniture and I'd like to play around with dimensions. For this, I want to be able to add an object (like a dowel, a steel tube, a 2x4, etc.) between two other parts and have that object automatically stretch while I move the other parts around. The tricky bit is maintaining its cross section so that it doesn't squish or twist and lose its intended dimensions. What's the easiest way to do this in Blender?

Here's the result of my attempt to illustrate what I have in mind. This is done with constraints and hooks but obviously it's not enough:

I suspect it might be easier with round dowels but what about 2x4s or let's say aluminum profiles of complex shape?

EDIT: For now I create one segment paths, hook their ends to the target objects and then in Object Data Properties > Geometry > Bevel set the desired cross section shape. I'm not sure how good this solution is but it works perfectly for dowels and I've yet to figure out how to set orientation for other shapes.
answer_html:
(Using Blender 4.2.9)

Overview

Two empties, children of the objects at both ends of the tube to create, define the axis of this object. Then a profile is extruded along this axis for a short length at mid-span. Eventually, the vertices at the ends of the generated mesh are projected in the axis direction onto the objects at both ends of the tube. Extrusion and projection are performed by a GeometryNodes modifier.


(Blender 4.2.9+)

Setup


Figure 1: Named objects defining the configuration, and the input panel of the "GeometryNodes" modifier attached to the default "Cube" (renamed "Tube").

Let "Grid S" and "Grid E" be the objects respectively at start and end of the tube to create (see Fig.1). For the demonstration, Grid meshes with 3x3 vertices are used. Let "Point S" and "Point E" be two empty objects. Each "Point" is bound to a specific vertex of the respective "Grid" as follows:

  • In Edit Mode, the vertex is selected.
  • The 3D cursor is moved to this vertex using Shift S Cursor to Selected.
  • In Object Mode, the empty is created at the 3D cursor position using the menu entry Add > Empty > Plain Axes.
  • In Edit Mode after reselecting the "Grid" object (the targeted vertex should be still selected), add the empty to the selection using Ctrl LMB.
  • The empty is bound to the vertex using the menu entry Vertex > Make Vertex Parent (shortcut Ctrl P).

The profile to extrude along the axis is made of a 2D Curve object, with Fill Mode set to None. Its position and orientation are irrelevant. A Cogwheel is used for the demonstration.

GeometryNodes modifier

This modifier is added to the default "Cube" object, whose initial mesh is irrelevant because it is completely discarded and replaced. The profile orientation and size are controlled by rotating and scaling this object, not the profile itself. The modifier inputs are (see Fig.1):

  • Profile: The Curve object to extrude.
  • Start/End Object: The objects at both ends of the tube.
  • Start/End Point: The empty objects defining the tube axis.


Figure 2: (top) Main graph. (bottom) Projection group node.


Figure 3: Intermediate result after the Curve to Mesh node, showing the Face Index.

Let $O$ be the origin of the object to which the modifier is attached, $S$ and $E$ be both ends of the tube axis, and $C$ be the mid-point of this axis.

Main graph
1. Vectors $\vec{OS}$ and $\vec{OE}$ are recovered through the Location socket of Object Info nodes. The Transform Space parameter is set to Relative to make the procedure independent of where is in 3D world coordinate system the origin of the object to which the modifier is attached.
2. The tube axis $\vec{SE}$, defining the extrusion/projection direction, is computed by subtracting $\vec{OS}$ from $\vec{OE}$.
3. The center of the tube $C$ is computed as the averaged position between $S$ and $E$. It is assumed that there is no intersection of the profile put at $C$ with the "Grid S" object.
4. Let $D$ be a point along the tube axis slightly offset from $C$ towards $E$. It is defined as:

$$ \vec{OD} = \vec{SE} \times \alpha + \vec{OC} $$ The Multiplier $\alpha$ is arbitrarily set to $0.01$, meaning that the distance between $C$ and $D$ is 1% of the distance between $S$ and $E$. $\alpha$ should be large enough to limit numerical round off errors, but also small enough to prevent the intersection of the profile put at $D$ with the "Grid E" object.
$\vec{SE}$, $\vec{OC}$ and $\vec{OD}$ are computed using Vector Math nodes.
5. The axis portion along which the profile is firstly extruded is made of a Curve Line between points $C$ and $D$.
6. The output mesh is initialized by extruding the user defined profile along the line made in step 5 using a Curve to Mesh node. The Fill Caps parameter is activated to generate two n-gons faces at both ends of the line. Those faces, which are the last two in the Face list (see Fig.3), are useful to separate vertices afterwards.
7. The profile Geometry is recovered through an Object Info node whose Transform Space parameter is set to Original. Otherwise the Relative position between the profile and the object to which the modifier is attached, is preserved.
8. Vertices generated in step 6 are moved onto the objects at both ends of the tube using the Projection group node twice.

Projection group node
Inputs are the oriented tube axis $\vec{SE}$ (as Direction), the vertices to move (as part of Geometry), the object to project onto (as Object) and which face of the tube to be projected (as menu Face).
10. The input menu Face is converted to a Boolean using a Menu Switch node, to control two standard Switch nodes, because multiple Menu Switch nodes can not be connected to the same socket (i.e. Face here).
11. The index of the face to be projected is the penultimate for the "Start" face and the last for the "End" face, following the order of the faces generated in step 6. Consequently because Index starts at 0, 2 for the "Start" face (resp. 1 for the "End" face) is subtracted using a Math node from the number of faces retrieved by a Domain Size node.
12. An Evaluate on Domain node set in Face domain is used to tag as True only the face whose Index matches the value computed in step 11.
13. The direction of projection is towards $S$ for the "Start" face and towards $E$ for the "End" face. Consequently to define the Ray Direction for the Raycast node, $\vec{SE}$ is multiplied by -1 for the "Start" face to invert it (resp. 1 for the "End" face to keep it unchanged).
14. It is assumed that the angle between the tube axis and the normal at the targeted object is not too flat, such that all the vertices can be projected at a distance lower than the length of the tube axis. This limit is computed as $\|\vec{SE}\|$ using a Vector Math node.
15. The Geometry of the object to project onto is recovered using an Object Info node set to Relative mode, as explained in step 1.
16. The vertices are projected using a Raycast node whose Hit Position output is the only one of interest. It is to notice that if there is no hit, the returned position is $(0,0,0)$. Consequently, such vertices are moved to the origin of the object to which the modifier is attached.
17. The position of the vertices is updated using a Set Position node. The Selection field is interpolated from the Face domain specified in step 12 to the Point domain used by this node, to transfer the True tag to the vertices to be projected. Indeed from the Boolean Domain Interpolation documentation, "A vertex is selected if any of the connected faces were selected.".

title: Zoom out camera using geometry nodes value
body_html:
I am looking for a way to have a camera in my scene get zoomed out using a (or multiple) value(s) retrieved from geometry nodes. Sadly I can not use the method used here due to the nature of my approach. The object generated in the scene has to stay the same scale while the camera zooms out, either through the usage of adjusting the focal length or moving it backwards in the XY transformation.

I have attempted to expose a value that calculates the distance between the closest edge to the camera and the center of the bounding box in the group output, but can't find a method to connect this to my camera.

Is it possible to achieve this through the usage of drivers or another method I might be missing here?
answer_html:
(Using Blender 4.2.1)

(NB: this answer is under writing...)

Objectives

There are two objectives:

  • To center the camera view inside the frame bounding the targeted object.
  • To adjust the camera focal length such that the targeted object is filling the camera view.


This animation illustrates how the view axis and focal length of the camera are evolving while its viewpoint and its orientation are modified.

Analysis

Let $O$ be the camera position, $T$ the central point the camera is looking at, $\vec{n}$ the camera view axis, $F$ the frame bounding the targeted object (i.e. the orange rectangle displayed on the right side of the above illustration).

  • $T$ is defined as the center of $F$ ; so $T$ is a function of $F$, $T=g(F)$.
  • $F$ is perpendicular to $\vec{n}$ with $\vec{n} = \vec{OT} / \|\vec{OT} \|$; so $F$ is a function of $T$, $F=h(T)$.

From Blender point of view, there is a circular dependency between $T$ and $F$. From a mathematical point of view, $T$ is a fixed point of the function $g \circ h$, i.e. $T=g \circ h(T)$. Assuming $T$ known, $g \circ h(T)$ is computed in two steps:

  • $F=h(T)$: The points of the targeted object are projected on the plane defined by $T$ and $\vec{n}$. Beware it is not a parallel projection, but a central projection of center $O$.
  • $T=g(F)$: $T$ is computed as the center of the bounding box of these projected points. The orientation of the bounding box is defined by the camera.

Approach

In numerical analysis, fixed-point iteration is a method of computing fixed points of a function. Let $i$ be the iteration counter. $T^{i+1}$, an intermediate value of $T$, is computed as $T^{i+1} = g \circ h(T^i)$. It is expected that $T^i$ converges towards $T$ for a given accuracy in a finite number of iterations. The recursion is initialized with $T^0$ set at the center of the targeted object bounding box.

In the frame of this question, this basic iteration process can be diverging when the distance between the camera and the targeted object is small compared to the object size (for more details, see Stationary iterative methods). To recover convergence, a relaxation technique is implemented, as a linear combination of the previous value $T^i$ with the new evaluation $T^{*}=g \circ h(T^i)$. Let $\alpha$ be the relaxation coefficient with $\alpha \in [0:1]$. $T^{i+1}$ is defined as: $$ T^{i+1} = \alpha \times T^i + (1-\alpha) \times T^{*}$$

This figure illustrates how the camera view (bounded by a black dash line) is converging with $\alpha=0.2$ for a configuration that is diverging otherwise without relaxation (i.e. $\alpha=0$). For demonstration purpose, the projected faces are superimposed in wire mode, and the "empty" space around is filled with rectangular faces (NB: the resulting grid is chosen slightly larger than the camera view for aesthetic reasons). After 1 iteration, "Suzanne" right eye is out of frame ; $T$ has to be moved to the left side. After 2 iterations, this eye is in frame, but the tip of its left hear is out of frame ; $T$ has to be moved back to the right side. Next iterations show such damped oscillations until convergence is reached.

Resources

  • Blender file: (Blender 4.2.1+)
  • To track only the center of the object bounding box, see: Take position values geometry nodes and apply them on an object outside of geometry nodes
  • The communication between GeometryNodes and Drivers is derived from the post Passing GeoNodes attribute to Shader frame offset.

Parts and chain of dependencies

To avoid circular dependencies, four "parts" are chained. These are described thereafter from the root, without dependency, to the most dependent.

  • Ouput (no dependency): The section Format of the Output Properties panel is defining the rendered image Resolution. The ratio between X and Y values fixes the camera view aspect ratio.
  • Observer (driven by Output): This object carrying the GeometryNodes modifier is computing and encoding the position of $T$, the camera Focal Length, the camera Sensor Width and the camera orientation. The focal length is adjusted to accommodate the width and height of the projected object. Thus the rendered image aspect ratio is required from the Output.
  • CameraData (driven by Observer): Through its position, this object is exposing the camera Focal Length and Sensor Width parameters. A Copy Location constraint is fixing its position from data coded by the Observer.
  • Camera (driven by Observer and CameraData): This object is a child of the Observer, which is controlling its position this way. Besides Damped Track and Locked Track constrains are fixing its orientation towards $T$ from data coded by the Observer. Eventually, drivers based on the CameraData object position are setting values in the Lens and Camera sections of the Camera Data Properties panel.

Setup

Observer

The Observer is a Mesh object made of only 3 vertices, from an edited Cube primitive for example. The position of these vertices is irrelevant as it is fixed by the GeometryNodes modifier. Each of these vertices is assigned to one Vertex Group. The first one named "Target" is coding the position of $T$. The second one named "CameraData" is coding the Focal Length (as X) and the Sensor Width (as Y) of the camera. The last one named "Top" is coding the position of the center of the upper edge of the camera view frame.

The input parameters of the GeometryNodes modifier are:

  • Object: the targeted object.
  • Sensor Width (mm): the size of the sensor determining the focal length of the camera.
  • Aspect Ratio: used to compute the height of the camera sensor from its width.
  • Iterations: number of fixed-point iterations.
  • Relaxation: relaxation coefficient $\alpha$.

CameraData

The CameraData is an Empty object whose initial position is irrelevant as it is fixed by the Copy Location constraint.

Camera

The Camera is a Camera object whose initial position is collocated with the origin of the Observer. It is parented to the Observer. Contrary to a classical setup, the viewpoint, the view orientation and scale are set by manipulating the Observer, not the Camera directly.

GeometryNodes modifier

Convergence and encoding

The following graph is attached to the Observer.

1. The fixed-point iterations with relaxation are performed by a Repeat Zone. Only the "Target" item is recycled ; as input, it is equal to $T^{i}$ ; as output, it is equal to $T^{i+1}$.
2. The "Frame" Group Node is computing $T^{*}=g \circ h(T^i)$ from the projection of the targeted object. It is also returning the "Top" position of the frame, as well as its dimensions, "Width" and "Height".
3. $T^0$ is computed as the average of the Min and Max positions returned by a Bounding Box node applied to the targeted object. It is to notice that the Transform Space of the Object Info node providing its Geometry is set to Relative. Consequently, subsequent vector geometry is performed with the point $O$ set at the origin of the Observer.
4. To encode ... (to be continued)

Computation

Mathematics

title: Geometry Nodes:"Distribute Points on Faces" vs "Set Material" selection discrepancy
body_html:
[I butchered the question with a heavy hand, you can still access the previous revision here - MVB]

I use the same field for Selection of those nodes:

  • Distribute Points on Faces
  • Set Material

and yet the first node distributes some points on faces, where a material wasn't set by the second node. What causes this discrepancy and how to fix it?

The Selection field:
answer_html:
From the docs:

Set Material

Selection

Whether to change the material of each face[…]

Distribute Points on Faces

Selection

The selection of which face corners[…]

Therefore the difference comes from the fields being evaluated in different domains: face vs face corner. Possible solutions:

  • using Evaluate on Domain node before one of the pair of problematic nodes, and switching the domain to the domain used by the other node,
  • capturing an attribute in face domain, and reading the captured attribute, as that face → face corner interpolation is an exact copy of a value,
  • setting a material first, and then using a material index for the selection.

title: Particle System on Procedural Plane
body_html:
I got problem with my procedural terrain and scatter grass. So, the purpose that I aiming to add scatter grass on my terrain (The green thing on the terrain is from shader object material not actually a scatter grass). But something wrong when I'm apply the particle system to the terrain. The terrain will be flattened after I add particle system.

This is what its looks like:

This is my terrain:

After applying particle system:

How to fix this? or there any alternative ways?

For more details, I have uploaded the file project here so anyone can see what is wrong with the project Click this to see more details about the project

So, another problem just appeared. The grass started to be floating in some position (especially on the high ground of the terrain) And this is what they look like:

And for the "Show" button, I have tried to check the button and they show the setup like this:

It seems like the cubes is floating too in some positions. How to fix this?
answer_html:
(Using Blender 4.2.5)

Figure 1: Bare ground.

Figure 2: Ground with grass. Setup: Vertices=33, Density=1, Scale=3.

Resources:

(Blender 4.2.5+)
(NB: Images for texturing are not packed to remain under the 30MB limit. These images can be found in the original file linked in the question.)

Analysis

In Blender workflow, modifiers are evaluated before shading nodes. Consequently, the ParticleSystem modifier is spawning grass over the flat ground, before the Displacement shading node is making the terrain elevation. Furthermore, adding a ParticleSystem modifier after the Subdivision modifier disables the Adaptive Subdivision parameter (yet an experimental feature in Blender 4.3). Consequently without this parameter checked, the number of subdivisions must be increased from 1 to 6 to match the first provided picture, otherwise "the terrain will be flattened".

Overview and setup

Figure 3: Setup and main GeometryNodes graph. The Spreadsheet Editor shows the objects instanced from the "Grass" collection.

The proposed approach is replacing the ParticleSystem modifier, attached to the "Ground" object, by a GeometryNodes modifier, attached to the default "Cube" renamed "Vegetation", which:

  • Builds an auxiliary grid the same size as the original ground object (see Auxiliary Grid group node),
  • Displaces this grid points to reproduce the large scale elevations made by the shading nodes on the original ground object (see Elevation group node),
  • Instances over this elevated grid the objects gathered in the "Grass" collection (see Spawner group node).

The auxiliary grid is not rendered, only the "Grass" collection objects are.

Input parameters are:

  • Object: The object to populate with grass. It is assumed it is an XY plane.
  • Vertices: Number of points of the auxiliary grid in X and Y directions. This value must be increased for high terrain slopes, large grass densities and low grass scales.
  • Collection: Objects to distribute over the auxiliary grid.
  • Density: The number of objects to distribute per square meter.
  • Scale: Scale to apply to the distributed objects.

GeometryNodes modifier

Auxiliary Grid group node

Figure 4: Graph generating the auxiliary grid, and recovering geometrical data of the "Ground" object.

1. The Object Info node recovering the data of the "Ground" object is set in Relative transform space to get this object transformations applied.
2. Its Scale in Z direction is used to scale the elevation.
3. The mid point of its Bounding Box is used to center the auxiliary grid on this object.
4. Its size in X and Y directions is computed from its Bounding Box corners.

Elevation group node

The terrain elevation procedure is duplicated between the shading nodes of the "Ground" object and the geometry nodes of the "Vegetation" object. It is the weakness of this approach because the structure of both graphs must matched. To minimize discrepancies, Drivers can be used to propagate parameters. In the Shader Editor, use RMB Copy as New Driver over a parameter, then in Geometry Node Editor, use RMB Paste Driver.

Figure 5: Shading nodes generating the terrain displacement.

Figure 6: Graph generating the elevation of the auxiliary grid. Parameters with light pink background are set by drivers.

Dark blue nodes: Computation of the generated texture coordinates
5. By construction in Auxiliary Grid group node, the Position $X$ (resp. $Y$) coordinate is between $-\frac{1}{2}\mathit{Size\ X}$ and $+\frac{1}{2}\mathit{Size\ X}$ (resp. $\mathit{Size\ Y}$). Consequently, $X/\mathit{Size\ X}+\frac{1}{2}$ is between 0 and 1.

Dark green nodes: Computation of the elevation height
6. The Mapping shading node is only applying a rotation. Thus it is replaced by a Vector Rotate node.
7. The unconnected Vector socket of a Noise Texture shading node is implicitly using the generated texture coordinates. Thus in geometry nodes, it has to be explicitly connected to the vector provided by the dark blue nodes, to overwrite the Position attribute implicitly used otherwise.
8. The setup of the Color Ramp and Mix nodes must be the identical between both editors.

Dark pink nodes: Conversion of height in displacement
9. The Displacement shading node is subtracting the Midlevel value from the Height, before multiplying by the Scale value.
10. In the proposed setup, the scale of the object to which the GeometryNodes modifier is attached is kept at the default value $(1,1,1)$. Consequently, the elevation of the auxiliary grid must be explicitly scaled by the Scale Z value of the "Ground" object.
11. The displacement is applied as an Offset in Z direction only, i.e. along the normal of the XY auxiliary grid.

Dark red nodes: Positioning of the auxiliary grid
12. Eventually, the auxiliary grid points are translated such that this grid center is collocated with the mid point of the bounding box of the "Ground" object, to comply with the definition of the generated texture coordinates.

Spawner group node

Figure 7: Graph instancing objects over the auxiliary grid (left), and illustration of the setup control, i.e. with "Show" sets True (right).

Dark red nodes:
13. Instancing positions are randomly drawn with a Distribute Points on Faces node.
14. The output Rotation is used to align the instanced objects X axis with the Mesh normal.

Dark green nodes:
15. The geometry of each grass patch is recovered using a Collection Info node. It is mandatory to tick the Separate Children and Reset Children parameters.
16. The Pick Instance parameter of the Instance on Points node is ticked also. It is to notice that it is useless to randomize the Instance Index because the position is already random.

Dark pink nodes:
17. A $\pm 20\%$ randomness is applied to the user defined Scale parameter to vary the grass patches size.

Dark blue nodes:
18. To debug the Elevation group node, Cubes can be instanced at each grid point instead (see Fig.(7 right)).

Edition

Figure 8: Graph instancing objects over the auxiliary grid (Updated Spawner group node).

Dark grey nodes:
19. To vary the grass patches orientation, a random rotation in $[-\pi:\pi]$ around Z axis is applied before patches are aligned with the mesh local normal. Because rotations do not commute, it is mandatory that the Z axis rotation is input first in the Rotate Rotation node.

You can try my setup if you want, I've described it here (ru language, you can try google translate if you want)

The core element is using rest position attribute, This is the node setup that I've used:

GN defines the distance between the points: the current one and the original one recorded in the Rest Position attribute. This is how the difference in edge lengths gets.

The result is saved to a new attribute, I called it "FaceArea" in the screenshot.

title: explain why geometry nodes positioning is acting more like scaling
body_html: Im struggling somewhat with geometry nodes to understand why some attributes work the way they do. In this video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nFtRnBErnmw&t=330s around minute 3:30 it shows how the capture attribute of position is going down to the center point of the geometry. Then pulling the value directly from the position node shows the position of the original mesh. What does running the position node through the capture attribute node do? Why when you mix them instead of moving the hexagons between the outer and center position it is scaling them? When I attach the viewer node to any of the position or store attribute I get an empty list in the spreadsheet screen.
answer_html:
Capture Attribute

This node is essential because field input nodes like the Position Node work in the context of the node they are connected to. (Official Blender documentation)

Without a Capture Attribute, the input node Position will return the position of each vertex/edge/face (depends on the context).

By passing the Position through a Capture Attribute set on Face, you are now getting the position of the face, which is the same for all 5 or 6 vertices of the face.

So, for each vertex, by mixing between the position of the vertex and the position of the face to which it belongs, you are attracting all 5 or 6 vertices to the center of the face. You are only playing between [position of vertices] and [position of face].

Here is a visualisation for one face, where face position is shown by cones.

So in your example, you are capturing the position of the face and using it on vertices.

Your questions

What does running the position node through the capture attribute node do ?

You are explicitly asking to get the Position from the point of view of a certain Domain (here, Face).

Why when you mix them instead of moving the hexagons between the outer and center position it is scaling them ?

You are not mixing between [vertex position] and [origin], but between [vertex position] and [face position]. You are only repositioning the vertices but you are correct, it is identical to scaling faces.

When I attach the viewer node to any of the position or store attribute I get an empty list in the spreadsheet screen.

You can set your Viewer to any Domain you want : face, vertex, ... Default is automatic and doesn't always give you what you are expecting.

My current tree uses split edges to create random islands, subdivides those islands (To control size of gap), and then deletes the outer edges of the islands.

It almost works the way I want, but only the faces using the selected edges are deleted, so when the islands have concave corners they leave a face there.

Basically trying to replicate the results of if you had selected a bunch of edges in edit mode, swapped to vertex select and pressed delete, all the faces using those selected vertices would be deleted, I need that functionality with geo nodes.

answer_html:
(Using Blender 3.6.8)

One approach is to tag split edges before subdivision, then to delete all points along these edges after subdivision.

1. The user-defined named attribute "to delete" is attached to each Edge and it is initialized to False by the first Store Named Attribute node.
2. The second Store Named Attribute node is setting the attribute "to delete" to True for some edges matching the selection mask, based on a random selection.
3. The attribute "to delete" is transferred to refined edges by the Subdivide Mesh node.
4. The attribute "to delete" is interpolated from Edge to Point domain, as required by the Delete Geometry node set in Point domain. Be aware that Boolean data type attributes have special rules for interpolation. As a consequence, a point is deleted if at least one of the edges it is connected to has the attribute "to delete" set to True.

title: Mapping Vertex Colors to -1 1
body_html:
I'm attempting to use vertex colors on a base mesh as an intuitive way to set hair curve displacement in Geometry Nodes using a simple Map Range to convert the 0—1 RGB data to -1—1 XYZ data. This works as expected with vertex groups, but not with vertex colors.

I saw this post (mapping normals from -1-1 to 0-1) which seems to be closely related, as I ended up with the same 0.735357 zero value as one of the answers pointed out.

Essentially, how would vertex colors be stored/retrieved/converted to plain RGB colorspace, bypassing the gamma correction?

EDIT: Demonstrative .blend

I've created a simple demo file to illustrate the problem. Here is a sphere with both a Vertex Color and Vertex Group attribute. Left side has a .5 value, middle is 0 and right is 1:

Vertex Group (float mask) mapped to -1 to 1:

Vertex Color (color mask) mapped to -1 to 1:

The vertex group example is the correct result. The value of .5 when mapped to -1 to 1 simply results in 0. The vertex color on the other hand, in this case the blue channel, isn't a true float value.
answer_html:
(Using Blender 4.2.7)

Overview

The RGB values defined by the user with Vertex Paint are nonlinear, whereas the RGB values stored in named attributes are linear. Therefore stored RGB values must be made nonlinear to retrieve the user defined RGB values. This transformation is named "Companding".

Figure 1: Results achieved by making stored RGB values nonlinear.

Resources:

(Blender 4.2.7+)

Analysis

In Blender documentation, "Scene Linear Color Space" and "Display Color Spaces" are explained. In short,

"Rendering and compositing is best done in scene linear color space, which corresponds more closely to nature, and makes computations more physically accurate. (...) However, these values do not directly correspond to human perception or the way display devices work. and image files are often stored in different color spaces."

Figure 2: Identification procedure: "Blue" value is specified in "Vertex Paint" workspace, and the associated named attribute "Hair.Displace.Colors" is displayed in "Spreadsheet Editor".

To identify how RGB values specified with Vertex Paint are stored as attribute, a Viewer node is linked to the output of the Separate Color node, and the object is uniformly painted (see Fig.2, illustrating that a user defined RGB value of 0.5 is stored as 0.212).

Figure 3: Conversion between nonlinear RGB values and linear rgb values (NB: rgb values are multiplied by 1000). Yellow background cells hold values entered in the "Vertex Paint" color panel ; blue background cells hold values returned by the Viewer node ; red background cells highlight mismatched values. Top arrow shows the "Companding" operation ; bottom arrows show the "Inverse Companding" operation.

The output for "RGB (float)" values between 0 and 1 is reported Fig.3. The "RGB (int)" column holds values coded as integers between 0 and 255, instead of floats between 0 and 1. The "int" value is computed by rounding to the nearest integer the multiplication of the "float" value by 255 (NB: N.5 is rounded to N ; e.g. 0.1 yields 25).

From the answer of Robert Gützkow to the question Mapping normals from -1..1 to 0..1, and comparing the "rgb (Blender)" value with the "rgb (int)" value computed from the "RGB (int)" value, it seems reasonable to assume that the stored RGB value is indeed the "Inverse Companding" of the specified RGB value (see the green arrow Fig.3). There are different RGB companding formulations. Blender seems to use the sRGB one, adapted as follows:

Inverse sRGB Companding: $$ \begin{array}{rcl} \overline{V} & = & \left\lfloor V \times 255 \right\rceil / 255 \\ v & = & \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \overline{V} / c & \textrm{if }\ \overline{V} \le d \\ \left[(\overline{V}+b)/a\right]^\gamma & \textrm{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \\ \end{array} $$

sRGB Companding: $$ V = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} c \times v & \textrm{if }\ c \times v \le d \\ a \times v^{1/\gamma} - b & \textrm{otherwise} \end{array} \right. $$

with

  • $\left\lfloor x \right\rceil$: $x$ rounded to the nearest integer.
  • $V$: one of the nonlinear RGB channels.
  • $\overline{V}$: truncated value of $V$ because of the conversion between the float interval $[0:1] \cap \mathbb{R}$, and the 8-bit integer interval $[0:255] \cap \mathbb{N}$.
  • $v$: one of the linear rgb channels.
  • $a, b, c, d, \gamma$: constant values specific to the sRGB color space: $$ \begin{array}{rcl} a & = & 1.055 \\ b & = & a-1 \\ c & = & 12.92 \\ d & = & 0.04045 = 40.45\ 10^{-3}\\ \gamma & = & 2.4 \\ \end{array} $$

$V$, $\overline{V}$ and $v$ are float numbers between 0 and 1. Values in italic Fig.3 are in the linear part (i.e. $V \le d$).

Figure 4: Comparison between the "Blue" value specified in "Vertex Paint" workspace, and the value recomputed from the associated named attribute "Hair.Displace.Colors" displayed in "Spreadsheet Editor".

It is to notice that because $\overline{V}$ can be different from $V$, there can be a mismatch between the user defined RGB value (first column in Fig.3) and the value recomputed from the stored attribute (last column in Fig.3) (see Fig.4).

GeometryNodes modifier

Figure 5: sRGB companding: group node converting the rgb linear value $v$ to the RGB nonlinear value $V$.

References

  • About Blender color spaces: see Color Management.
  • About sRGB color space: see sRGB.
  • About conversion between color spaces: see Bruce Lindbloom pages.

title: How to generate points based on curve roots in geometry nodes?
body_html:
How to generate geometry points based on curve roots in Geometry Nodes? I tried, but it doesn't work.

Generated to 0, 0, 0.
answer_html:
It does not work because Field values (the diamond slots with the dotted lines) depend on the Geometry (the green connections & green nodes) that they are connected to. You need to read it from right to the left (Field values (what) <= Geometry (from where/context)).

In your screenshot you have connected the Curve Root node group to the Points geometry node. This actually means, that you ask the points for their curve root position. Since points are no curves, they tell you: "Silly you, we are points! We have no root position!" and you get (0, 0, 0).

What you actually want is the root position of curves and they should be transfered to the new created points. The position is the position of the control points of the splines in the Curve domain. The new created points are in Point Cloud domain. That's two different geometry types.

Transfer the Position Attribute

A common way to transfer an attribute between domains, is to capture the attribute with a Capture Attribute node on the specific domain/geometry and map it to the destination with a Sample ... node.

When you have a matching number of curves and points you can use the Sample Index node. This way, Blender will assign the 1st position to the 1st point, the 2nd position to the 2nd point, etc. using their index values. Here is an example:

Oh, wait. You can simplify this a bit and use the Root Position value:

Both versions work because Position/Root Position is connected to the Capture Attribute node that is conneted to the geometry of the curves. Since the domain of Capture Attribute is set to Point, the position of the control points and not the curves is retrieved.

Alternatively, Copy and Convert the Root Control Points

Another approach to solve your problem is to copy the Control Points of the curve and convert them into Point Cloud points. Additionally, you need to adjust the point radius a bit to get the exact same result.

body_html: Blender 3.2 - "Point Instance" Node. Is this available or did the name change?
answer_html:
With Blender 3.0, the Point Instance node has been replaced by the Instance on Points node.

The following options have been added:

  • Via Selection it can be selected at which points an instantiation should take place.
  • Not only single objects can be instantiated, but also whole collections.
  • With Pick Instance and Instance Index it can be influenced which objects from the collection are to be instantiated.
  • Furthermore, there is the possibility to apply a rotation and a scaling directly during the instantiation.

  1. When we store the position of an object in ‘test’, does Blender still recognize it as a position?

  3. When we pass the "test" to the ‘checkered texture’ in Blender, does it perform an implicit conversion to UV maps?
answer_html:
First of all you have to understand that there are different data types in Blender, like float, vector, integer and so on. Second you have to understand that Blender converts these types automatically "inside" as Blender needs it. As you can imagine it is not very hard for Blender e.g. to convert vector to a color (without alpha) because both are just 3 float values. So x will become R, y will become G and z will become B (xyz -> RGB). (more info:https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/interface/controls/nodes/parts.html) Blender "knows" each data type, so it knows also the data type of all attributes (and you have to tell Blender which data type you wanna store). So you do store a vector (attribute) to all points in your geometry by "store named attribute"-node. For Blender - it is just a vector. Not a position. You can now "use" this vector as color (if you want to) but also as position or uv coordinate. You decide what to do with that vector. And by using/reading it via shader nodes in attribute and plugging it into the checker vector, you "decide" to use the vector as position. If you plug that same vector into color1, you "decide" to use the vector as color.

For Blender it is still and will always be just a vector (3 float values in an array). Nothing else. You decide how to use that.

Hope that helps a bit.

title: Noise not showing in GeoNodes when grid size is multiple of face size. Why?
body_html:
I've made a blender GeoNodes setup where you can input single face size and entire grid size, then offsetting with a noise texture. It's for procedural terrain generation with consistent face size no matter how large.

But when I choose multiples like

Face size: 2m / Grid size: 8m

then the Noise doesn't show up. Shortly before and after the multiples it fades out when I slowly change the grid size.

I know it has something to do with the noise algorithm but dunno why. Can somebody explain?

Not showing up:

Here you see it working perfectly (when not using multiples):
answer_html:
This is an unfortunate side effect of how Noise Texture produces its values. At whole-number Scale numbers with no Distortion, it gives out a flat value of $0.5$. Here's the technical explanation directly from the manual:

While the noise is random in nature, it follows a certain pattern that might not evaluate to random values in some configurations. ... To understand why this happens, let us look at the following plot of a 1D noise texture:

The horizontal line denotes a value of 0.5 and the vertical lines denotes whole numbers assuming a noise scale of 1. As can be seen, the noise always intersects the 0.5 line at whole numbers. Since the aforementioned objects were distributed on a grid and have whole number locations, they all evaluate to 0.5. Which explains the issue at hand.

Generally, any discrete evaluation of noise at integer multiples of the reciprocal of the noise scale will always evaluate to 0.5. It also follows that evaluations closer to that will have values close to 0.5. In such cases, it is almost always preferred to use the White Noise Texture.

Regardless, one can mitigate this issue in a number of ways:

  • Adjust the scale of the noise to avoid aligning the noise with the evaluation domain.
  • Add an arbitrary offset to the texture coordinates to break the alignment with the evaluation domain.
  • Evaluate the noise at a higher dimension and adjust the extra dimension until a satisfactory result is achieved.

You have your Scale at an integer ($5.0$) and your Distortion at $0.0$, and you're using the Fac socket (meaning, single float numbers instead of vectors) so all you're getting is the number $0.5$ for all your vertices. When you don't use whole numbers for your face size your mesh grid doesn't align with the noise grid so you get differing values as expected. In short, change any of these whole numbers in any of the settings, or use the Color (vector) socket instead of Fac, and you'll get the usual displacement. It's just something you'll have to keep at the back of your mind when using a Noise Texture:

2021-01-16T11:42:49     WARNING    Cannot open C:/Users/User/Desktop/GBG_slope.tif.()

answer_html:
When you search for Polygonize in the Processing Toolbox, there appear several tools.

1) Polygonize tool converts line layer to polygon layer, turning an area inside three line segments into a polygon. This tool takes line vector layers as input.

2) Polygonize (raster to vector) converts raster into vector polygons. If adjacent pixels have same value, they are grouped into the same polygon.

**3) Raster pixels to polygons** creates a rectangle polygon for each raster pixel. Similar tool Raster pixels to points creates a centroid point for each raster pixel.

So the tool you need would probably be Polygonize (raster to vector). However, you would better reclassify your raster into reasonable number of classes before doing Polygonize operation.

title: QGIS Batch Process to save bands of a raster layer as separate raster files
body_html: I have a .tif file with 61 bands. Normally, to save a band, I use the rastar calculator expression filename@1. But since there are 61 bands, with each band corresponding to a date, from April 1 to May 31, is there a way to export all the 61 bands into 61 .tif files, like running it as a batch process?
answer_html:
Easy solution: Rearrange bands

Easier than the raster calculator for your task is the algorithm Rearrange bands.

  1. Run it from Menu Processing -> Toolbox in batch mode (old docu, doesn't show all options).

  2. Add bands 1 to 61: in the second column Selected band(s), click Autofill -> Add values by Expression, then enter the expression: generate_series (1,61). This automatically adds 61 lines (bands 1 to 61).

  3. In the first line, fill in the values for Input layer and Converted (path/filename). Then copy these values to the remaining 60 lines with Autofill... -> Fill down. Run it and you're done.

Generate filenames with the date represented in the raster band

When you save the rasters, you might want to automatically name the resulting files with the date that each band respresents. As long as there is a logical pattern between band no. and date, you can also use Autofill... -> Add values by expression. The following expression shows how to generate a filename where band no. 1 is april 1st 2024; band 2 is april 2nd etc.:

array_foreach(
    generate_series(0,61),
    'C:/Users/your_path/'  ||  -- replace with your path
    to_date ('2024-04-01','yyyy-MM-dd') + 
    to_interval (@element || ' day') || 
    '.tif'
)

Filenames generated automatically:

Variant: Raster Calculator

You could still do it with the raster calculator.

  1. Open the `Raster Calculator from Menu Processing -> Toolbox: then you have a button to run it in batch mode.

  2. Second column Expression, use Autofill -> Add values by Expression and enter this expression

    be sure you have the single ' and double quotes " exactly as below:

    array_foreach(
    generate_series (1, 61),
    '"filename@'  ||  @element  || '"'
)

  3. Fill in the first row of the other settings accordingly as in the first solution.

But since there are 61 bands, with each band corresponding to a date, from April 1 to May 31, is there a way to export all the 61 bands into 61 .tif files, like running it as a batch process?

title: Calculating the raster counts within overlapping polygon in QGIS
body_html:
I have a raster with land use classes (see image). I want to count the pixel values (i.e. the classes) within the blue perimeter. In QGIS, there is a tool called "Raster layer unique values report" which can be used to count pixel values.

However, it is not possible to select a vector layer to only count the unique values within a specific polygon. As such, I get the pixel counts for the entire raster.

Is it possible to only count the pixel values from a raster within a polygon in QGIS?
answer_html:
The Zonal Histogram tool using a polygon layer as input will give a new version of the polygon layer with a column for each raster value containing its count

Alternatively, you can use PyQGIS to clip the raster by the mask polygon, and then access the pixel counts through its data provider:

poly = QgsProject.instance().mapLayersByName('my polygon')[0]

rast = 'path/to/raster'

## clip raster to polygon
rast_clipped = processing.run("gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer", {'INPUT':rast,'MASK':poly,'SOURCE_CRS':None,'TARGET_CRS':None,'NODATA':None,'ALPHA_BAND':False,'CROP_TO_CUTLINE':True,'KEEP_RESOLUTION':False,'SET_RESOLUTION':False,'X_RESOLUTION':None,'Y_RESOLUTION':None,'MULTITHREADING':False,'OPTIONS':'','DATA_TYPE':0,'EXTRA':'','OUTPUT':'C:/temp/myClippedRaster.tif'})['OUTPUT']

## make a layer from the clipped raster path
rast_clipped = QgsRasterLayer(rast_clipped, 'rast_clipped')

## get the extent of the layer
extent = rast_clipped.extent()

## access the data provider
prov = rast_clipped.dataProvider()

## get histogram from data provider
## bin count 0 means it will create the most appropriate number of bins, minimum and maximum are the limits of the raster values you wish to count
hist = prov.histogram(bandNo=1, binCount=0, minimum=1, maximum=7, extent=extent, sampleSize=0, includeOutOfRange=False, feedback=None)

## get list of counts corresponding with bins (for a categorical raster these correspond with an ordered list of the class values)
counts = hist.histogramVector

print(counts)

> [2893, 46778, 21800, 4, 0, 245943, 26932]

title: Sampling points in raster without generating new file in QGIS
body_html:
I am aware that there are tools available in QGIS for sampling a raster at any given point from a shapefile.

The methods I've tried are:

  • Point sampling tool plugin
  • Raster analysis > sample raster values
  • Saga > Raster Values to Points

They all generate an output file, which contains the points and the altitude as an attribute (I always sample from a DEM).

Now, my workflow involves the constant change of a point shapefile, and then getting the Z values (by sampling a DEM), so end up generating a lot of trash files. Further, this implies also that I have to keep changing the path in my code for the new updated point file with the new altitudes.

Is there a tool I could use to sample a raster by just updating an attribute in the attribute table of the point shapefile?
answer_html:
You can use the raster_value function in an expression in the Field Calculator to update a field in your point layer with the pixel value from an underlying raster:

raster_value( 'DEM', 1,  $geometry )

Where 'DEM' is the name of your raster layer, and 1 is the band number.

You could also use this expression in a virtual field so that the value will be updated on the fly if you add or edit point features.
